design_detail: PET follow-up of dopamine transporter (DAT) availability ([11C]d-threo-methylphenidate). Five people with methamphetamine dependence were scanned in early abstinence (mean 3 months) and again in protracted abstinence (mean 14 months); 5 more were scanned once after at least 9 months; both were compared cross-sectionally with 11 non-using controls and with the earlier short-abstinence group of 12. Motor and memory tests were repeated in the 5 retested users only.
can_establish: That striatal DAT availability rose between early and protracted abstinence in the 5 users who stayed abstinent and were rescanned, and that the protracted-abstinence group did not differ significantly from controls in this small sample.
cannot_establish: That DAT recovery is typical of people who stop using (the 5 retested were a selected subgroup with higher baseline DAT); whether the increase is regrowth, re-expression or something else; that cognition does or does not recover (5 people, no retested control group, no normative comparison); or equivalence with controls (a non-significant difference in 10 vs 11 people).

sample.recruitment: Users enrolled in a California drug-court monitoring rehabilitation programme with weekly or biweekly drug screens; controls by advertisement (p. 9415).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence; average use of at least 0.25 g/day, at least 5 days a week, for at least 2 years; at least 2 weeks' abstinence. Excluded: HIV seropositivity, comorbid neuropsychiatric disorder, medical illness, dependence on drugs other than methamphetamine and nicotine (p. 9415).
sample.demographics: Retested users: 3 women, 2 men, age 29 (SD 3). Users tested once: 4 women, 1 man, age 35 (SD 3). Controls: 7 women, 4 men, age 31 (SD 7). Short-abstinence group of 12: 7 women, 5 men, age 30 (SD 6) (p. 9415). Education, IQ and smoking not reported.
sample.attrition: Of the 12 users scanned in early abstinence, only the 5 who stayed drug-free for at least 9 months were rescanned; the other 7 dropped out of the programme and probably relapsed (pp. 9414–9415).
sample.selection_effects: Strong: at the first scan the 5 who later stayed abstinent already had higher DAT than the 7 who dropped out (putamen 1.74 vs 1.40, p<0.03; caudate 1.48 vs 1.20, p<0.07) and performed better on the pegboard and delayed recall (p. 9416). The recovery data therefore come from the users who were least affected to begin with. Participants were in a drug-court programme in which, as described for the same programme by Wang et al. (2004, p. 247), relapse meant a return to jail: a particular population.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported history; abstinence monitored with weekly or biweekly drug screens in the programme and a urine test before each scan (p. 9415).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Inclusion threshold 0.25 g/day, 5 days/week, 2 years (p. 9415); individual doses and years are used in correlations but not tabulated.
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other drugs except nicotine excluded; other use not quantified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Retested users: 3 months (SD 1.6) at first scan, 14 months (SD 2) at second. Users tested once: 17 months (SD 10). Short-abstinence group: 64 days (SD 40) (p. 9415; Table 1, p. 9416).

comparison.controls: 11 non-using volunteers recruited by advertisement, scanned once (p. 9415).
comparison.matching: Similar age and sex mix; not matched on education, IQ or smoking (not reported).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; baseline here is early abstinence, not pre-exposure.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: No history of drug abuse except nicotine or caffeine (p. 9415).

outcomes.instruments: DAT availability (Bmax/Kd) in caudate and putamen; K1 as a delivery check (p. 9415). Timed Gait, Grooved Pegboard and Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (immediate, delayed, interference recall) in the retested users only (p. 9415).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neuropsychological scores were compared neither with controls nor with norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Recovery = within-person increase in DAT between scans; 'functional recovery' = within-person change in test scores.

analysis.effect_sizes: Retested users: DAT +19% in caudate (p<0.003) and +16% in putamen (p<0.05), paired tests (p. 9415; Figure 2). Cross-sectional (Table 1, p. 9416): controls caudate 1.76 (SD 0.27), putamen 1.97 (SD 0.21); short abstinence (n=12) 1.32 (SD 0.28) and 1.56 (SD 0.30); protracted abstinence (n=10) 1.67 (SD 0.29) and 1.80 (SD 0.35). Short abstinence was 26% (caudate) and 21% (putamen) below controls; protracted abstinence 5% and 9% below, not significant (p. 9416). Editors' calculation from Table 1: protracted vs controls d≈−0.3 (caudate) and −0.6 (putamen), so 'not different' reflects low power, not demonstrated equivalence. DAT increase correlated with days between scans r=0.92 (n=5; 95% interval about 0.20–0.99, editors' calculation) and, in putamen, with reported dose r=0.88 (described as negative; interval about −0.01 to 0.99) (p. 9416, Figure 3). Tests: Timed Gait 10.0 to 8.6 s (p<0.13), delayed recall 11.6 to 12.8 words (p<0.10); no change in pegboard, immediate or interference recall; correlations of DAT change with test change r=0.78 (p<0.12) and r=0.71 (p<0.18) (pp. 9415–9416).
analysis.selective_reporting: Neuropsychological means are given only for the 2 tests with trends; the others are reported as unchanged without values.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors acknowledge the small sample limits the neuropsychological analysis (p. 9418).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 5 selected users who stayed abstinent, striatal DAT rose by about a sixth between early and protracted abstinence; in 10 users scanned in protracted abstinence, DAT was not significantly below that of 11 controls. Motor and memory scores in the 5 showed non-significant trends towards improvement.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and a section heading state that neuropsychological function did not recover and that the DAT increase was not sufficient for complete functional recovery (abstract, p. 9414; heading, p. 9417), although the text concedes the failure to see an association could reflect the small sample (p. 9418) and no comparison with controls or norms was made. The dropouts' lower baseline DAT is read as 'less DA terminal damage' in those who stayed abstinent (p. 9418), which presupposes the damage interpretation the paper elsewhere leaves open (p. 9417).

timeline.event: Baseline study of the larger sample: DAT 28% (caudate) and 21% (putamen) lower than controls; it inferred no significant recovery within a year
Metabolism follow-up in the same programme: thalamic but not striatal metabolism partly recovered
Critical review notes that duration of abstinence appears to have little effect on cognitive performance across studies, and that one later PET study did not find DAT recovery (McCann et al., 2008)
Review notes the increase is unlikely to be a test–retest artefact but no control group was rescanned

replication.where_it_stands: DAT increases with abstinence were also reported in a small SPECT study with a retested control group (Chou et al., 2007, summarized by Dean et al., 2013, p. 265), while McCann et al. (2008) found no relation between abstinence and DAT (Hart et al., 2012, p. 597). No large, longitudinal, control-retested study exists.

funding.funder: US Department of Energy Office of Biological and Environmental Research; National Institute on Drug Abuse grants; NIH General Clinical Research Center grants (Harbor-UCLA and Stony Brook); Office of National Drug Control Policy (p. 9414).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Same group and programme as Volkow et al. (2001a, 2001c) and Wang et al. (2004).

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people starting treatment, scanned and tested repeatedly over 1–2 years whether or not they stay abstinent, with non-using controls rescanned and retested at the same intervals, so that recovery, practice effects and selection can be separated.

domains.note: No adjustment; smoking, education and other drug use not reported.
Abstinence monitored in a drug-court programme; amounts self-reported.
Only the 5 of 12 who stayed abstinent were rescanned, and they differed at baseline in DAT and test scores.
Rehabilitation, cognitive behaviour therapy and the threat of jail on relapse (described for the same programme by Wang et al., 2004, p. 247) may themselves affect outcomes.
PET objective, but no rescanned controls for test–retest variation; no blinding reported; neuropsychological retesting without a practice-effect control.
Only trending tests reported with values.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person DAT increase is a real observation in 5 people, but it cannot be generalized: the retested users were selected by staying abstinent and already differed at baseline. The neuropsychological conclusions are not supported in either direction.

key_findings.finding: In 5 users rescanned after 14 months (vs 3 months) of abstinence, DAT availability rose 19% in the caudate and 16% in the putamen.
Cross-sectionally, users in short abstinence (n=12) had DAT 26% (caudate) and 21% (putamen) below controls (n=11); users in protracted abstinence (n=10) were 5% and 9% below, not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'Comparison between controls and METH abusers'; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: protracted vs controls d≈−0.3 and −0.6; underpowered, not equivalence.

key_findings.finding: The 5 who stayed abstinent had higher baseline DAT than the 7 who dropped out (putamen 1.74 vs 1.40, p<0.03) and better pegboard and delayed-recall scores.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'Comparison between METH abusers who dropped out…'

key_findings.finding: Timed Gait and delayed recall showed non-significant trends toward improvement (p<0.13, p<0.10); other tests unchanged; correlations of DAT change with test change were not significant.
The DAT increase correlated with the time between scans (r=0.92, n=5).
The authors list three explanations for the increase: down-regulation that reverses, terminal damage that recovers, or sprouting of remaining terminals.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations in 5 people are reported with df=4; the expected value is n−2=3.
reporting_issues.consequence: With df=3, r=0.88 has p≈0.05; the dose correlation is borderline.

reporting_issues.issue: The putamen DAT change is described as negatively correlated with dose and years of use, but the coefficients are printed as positive (r=0.88, r=0.83).
reporting_issues.consequence: Direction must be taken from the text and Figure 3A.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion threshold here is 0.25 g/day (p. 9415), while the baseline paper on the same programme states 0.5 g/day (Volkow et al., 2001a, p. 378).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two papers describe the same sample with different criteria.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and a section heading state that neuropsychological function did not recover; the data are non-significant trends in 5 people without a control comparison.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of a significant change is presented as evidence of no recovery.
